players.product: High-capacity nearline HDDs (UltraSMR / EPMR / HAMR) for AI capacity-tier storage

quarterly_data.signal: Q2 FY2026 results (CFO Kris Sennesael): revenue was $3 billion, up 25% year-over-year, 'driven by strong demand for our nearline drives'; EPS $2.13, up 78% year-over-year; both revenue and EPS were above the high end of the guidance range. Western Digital delivered 215 exabytes (up 22% year-over-year), including over 3.5 million drives or 103 exabytes of its latest-generation ePMR with capacity points up to 32 terabytes. Cloud was 89% of revenue at $2.7 billion (up 28% year-over-year); Client 6% at $176 million (up 26%); Consumer 5% at $168 million (down 3%). Gross margin was 46.1%, up 770 basis points year-over-year and 220 basis points sequentially, on the mix shift toward higher-capacity drives and tight cost control in manufacturing and the supply chain; opex $372 million; operating income slightly above $1 billion for an operating margin of 33.8%.
quarterly_data.figure: revenue was $3 billion, up 25% year-over-year; EPS $2.13; 215 exabytes, up 22%; Cloud 89% of total revenue at $2.7 billion, up 28%; gross margin 46.1%; operating margin of 33.8%

quarterly_data.signal: Outlook for the third quarter of fiscal 2026 (CFO): revenue of $3.2 billion, plus/minus $100 million, which at the midpoint reflects growth of approximately 40% year-over-year; gross margin between 47% and 48% (47.5% at the midpoint, up 740 basis points year-over-year); operating expenses of $380 million to $390 million; interest and other expenses approximately $50 million; tax rate approximately 16%; diluted EPS of $2.30, plus/minus $0.15 on approximately 385 million shares. Management said the guidance should 'underscore continued favorable trends in our business'.
quarterly_data.figure: next-quarter guide: revenue $3.2 billion, plus/minus $100 million (approximately 40% year-over-year at midpoint); gross margin 47% and 48%; EPS $2.30, plus/minus $0.15

quarterly_data.signal: HDD CAPACITY SOLD OUT FOR 2026, WITH LTAs INTO 2027-2028: CEO Irving Tan said 'we're pretty much sold out for calendar '26' - Western Digital has firm purchase orders with its top seven customers through calendar year 2026, and robust commercial agreements with three of its top five customers, two through calendar year 2027 and one through calendar year 2028. Asked whether those LTAs are volume-only, he clarified: 'These LTAs have both price and volume conditions in them.' He tied the longer contracts to a customer-centric reorganization around the big hyperscale customers 'with dedicated teams for each of them', better visibility into their demand, and a 'structural shift in the value that we deliver' to hyperscaler TCO as workloads move toward inference; customers want predictable pricing because of 'the high volatility of some tiers of the storage space'.
quarterly_data.figure: firm purchase orders with our top seven customers through calendar year 2026; two through calendar year 2027 and one through calendar year 2028

quarterly_data.signal: PRICING STABLE-TO-UP, COST DOWN ~10%: CFO Sennesael described 'a stable pricing environment with prices on a price per terabyte kind of flattish to slightly up', noting that last quarter it 'was up 2%, 3% on an ASP per terabyte basis'; CEO Tan added that pricing in the cloud segment was up single digit both last quarter and year-on-year, calling it a growth driver 'for the year and probably for the next two years as well'. On cost, cost per terabyte came down on or about 10% year-over-year, helped by upshifting customers to higher-capacity drives and manufacturing/supply-chain execution; Sennesael called on or about 10% 'a good number' that could go higher if roadmaps accelerate. The incremental gross margin is on or about 75%, versus his stated comfort level of anything higher than 50%, and he expects further gross margin expansion over the next couple of quarters and beyond.
quarterly_data.figure: price per terabyte kind of flattish to slightly up; up 2%, 3% on an ASP per terabyte basis; cost per terabyte was coming down on or about 10%; incremental gross margin is on or about 75%

quarterly_data.signal: HAMR QUALIFICATION PULLED IN, NEXT-GEN ePMR IN QUALIFICATION: CEO Tan said Western Digital pulled HAMR qualification forward to the first half of calendar '26 ('We've pulled in the qualification already by half year') and has already started qualification with one hyperscale customer this month, with a second hyperscale customer qualification starting 'imminently'. Qualification of next-generation ePMR drives has also started, with a different hyperscale customer; the Rochester SIT Lab supports fast qualification. The HAMR ramp is anticipated 'at the start of calendar year '27', and once HAMR reaches ePMR scale its gross margin is expected to be neutral to accretive versus ePMR (CFO: HAMR has been in development 'for the last 10 years'). Current-generation ePMR (up to 26 terabyte CMR and 32 terabyte UltraSMR) is 'yielding very well in the low 90s percentage yield range'; after over 3.5 million units last quarter, 'this quarter, we're looking to deliver close to 4 million drives.' Updated HAMR and ePMR roadmaps were to be shown at the Innovation Day on February 3rd in New York.
quarterly_data.figure: HAMR qualification pulled forward to the first half of calendar '26 with one hyperscale customer (second imminent); HAMR ramp at the start of calendar year '27; ePMR yields in the low 90s percentage; close to 4 million drives this quarter

quarterly_data.signal: HAMR LASER IN-SOURCING: CEO Tan said Western Digital 'recently acquired intellectual property assets and talent that will help us in the development of our internal laser capabilities' to accelerate HAMR. Terms are confidential. He said the technology takes 'much less real estate in the drive', helping manufacturability and reliability, and that 'energy requirements to support the lasers will also be reduced compared to the conventional laser diodes.'

UltraSMR PAST HALF OF NEARLINE MIX: CEO Tan said that last quarter Western Digital 'crossed on the nearline portfolio, 50% mix on UltraSMR' and expects that share to keep rising. Its top three customers are 'fully on board' with UltraSMR drives and another two to three are moving to adopt it. UltraSMR gives a 20% capacity uplift over CMR and a 10% capacity uplift over industry standard SMR, and because it is 'a software-based solution' it is 'very accretive for us from a margin standpoint'. Western Digital also announced UltraSMR-enabled JBOD platforms with software ecosystem partners, expanding UltraSMR adoption to a broader customer set.
quarterly_data.figure: 50% mix on UltraSMR (nearline portfolio); top three customers fully on board; another two to three more adopting; 20% capacity uplift over CMR; 10% capacity uplift over industry standard SMR

quarterly_data.signal: CASH, CAPEX AND CAPITAL RETURN (CFO): operating cash flow $745 million and capital expenditures $92 million gave free cash flow of $653 million, a 21.6% margin. Cash was $2 billion and total liquidity $3.2 billion; debt of $4.7 billion meant net debt of $2.7 billion. Share repurchases rose to $615 million (3.8 million shares) plus $48 million of dividends; $1.4 billion has been returned since the capital return program launched in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2025, and $1.3 billion of the $2 billion authorization has been used. A quarterly dividend of $0.125 per share was declared. The remaining 7.5 million SanDisk shares are to be monetized before the one-year anniversary of the separation, likely via a debt-for-equity swap, with proceeds used to reduce debt. CEO Tan: even with the HAMR ramp at the start of calendar year '27, CapEx as a percentage of revenue on a run-rate basis will stay within the 4% to 6% range. Separately, Western Digital announced a strategic investment in Qolab (quantum hardware) as an incubated growth vector.
quarterly_data.figure: capital expenditures were $92 million; free cash flow of $653 million (21.6%); CapEx within the 4% to 6% range of revenue; share repurchases to $615 million; 7.5 million SanDisk shares to monetize

quarterly_data.signal: AI INFERENCE AS THE STORAGE DEMAND ENGINE: CEO Tan said AI inference is 'becoming the true AI workload' and physical AI (autonomous vehicles, robotics) is producing ever-larger multimodal models, all of which need data. answering an analyst who cited the long-term exabyte CAGR of low 20s, Tan said Western Digital has 'seen exabyte growth over the last few quarters in the low 20s, as you've highlighted', and as AI value shifts from training to inference more data is created and stored - much of it on hard drives, since hyperscalers move data across tiers of SSDs, HDDs and tape - so 'inference is definitely going to drive a significant amount of data storage requirement'. Asked about NVIDIA's KV-cache offload work (analyst's framing), Tan said 'the initiative that NVIDIA has been driving is really to help accelerate inference capability', which will raise the velocity and volume of data and require more storage where HDDs have superior economics; Western Digital is working on innovations to improve drive bandwidth and throughput, to be detailed at its Innovation Day.
